findings.title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, likely a test leftover
findings.body: The cleanup loop's ticker was reduced from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. Nothing in the PR description or the annotations-cleanup change requires this; it looks like a debug leftover used while testing. This makes every cleanup job run 10x more often (temp files, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, temp users, short URLs, and the query-history row-limit enforcement of 200k/150k rows), sharply increasing DB and IO load on large deployments. If the intent was to compensate for possible under-deletion in the annotations job, that should be scoped to annotations only and documented, not applied to the global ticker.

findings.title: Routine cleanup progress is logged at Error level with full ID slices and a nil err
findings.body: All six new log lines (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) use `r.log.Error(...)` for normal per-batch progress, and each logs the entire `ids` slice (up to the configured batch size) plus `"err", err`. The first log of each pair always passes `err` from `fetchIDs` after it has already been nil-checked, so it emits an ERROR line with `err=nil`; the second logs the delete error, which is also returned to the caller. Consequences: cleanup now floods the error log on every cycle (and with the ticker change, every minute), formatting potentially tens of thousands of IDs per line, which wastes CPU/memory and produces false ERROR signals that will trigger alerting. These should be Debug-level messages and should not dump the full ID list or log a nil error.

findings.title: SQLite inline-ID branch builds the value list in O(n^2) time
findings.body: In the SQLite path of `deleteByIDs`, the ID list is built incrementally with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)`. Each iteration allocates and copies the entire growing string, so building a list of n IDs is O(n^2) in bytes copied. The newly added test deliberately exercises batch size 32767, where this copies on the order of gigabytes per delete and dominates the runtime; with large configured batch sizes it also burns real CPU in production. Use a `strings.Builder` (or `strconv.AppendInt` into a byte slice) to build the list in linear time.

findings.title: Only SQLite's bind-parameter limit is handled; large batches on MySQL/Postgres can exceed the placeholder limit
findings.body: `deleteByIDs` special-cases SQLite (over 999 parameters are inlined) but otherwise emits `len(ids)` `?` placeholders. `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` is a configurable value and `fetchIDs` can return up to that many IDs, so with a large configured batch size on MySQL or Postgres the generated DELETE can exceed the driver/server placeholder limit (commonly 65535) and fail with "too many placeholders"/"bind message has N parameter formats". Either cap/validate the batch size or apply the same inline / chunking strategy for all dialects.

findings.title: Annotation cleanup tests are now skipped under -short, removing short-mode coverage
findings.body: `TestAnnotationCleanUp` and `TestOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst` were renamed to `TestIntegration...` and now `t.Skip` when `testing.Short()` is set. Previously these DB-backed tests ran in short mode (they use the in-memory/test DB via `db.InitTestDB`), so they were the only coverage for the batched cleanup logic. After this change, short-mode CI runs no longer exercise `CleanAnnotations`, `fetchIDs`, `deleteByIDs`, or `untilDoneOrCancelled` at all. If the intent is to move them to integration CI, that is fine, but it should be confirmed that a non-short job actually runs this package, otherwise the rewritten cleanup path is effectively untested in most CI runs.
